insider_note: The integrating factor e^(Tan⁻¹x) multiplies the right side to give e^(2Tan⁻¹x), so the substitution t = Tan⁻¹x is what turns the final integral into a plain ∫e^(2t)dt rather than something left in x.

steps.label: Rewrite in standard form and identify P
steps.margin_note: One mark. Divide by (1 + x²) to reach the standard linear form.
steps.memory_tip: ∫1/(1+x²) dx = Tan⁻¹x — one of the standard integrals worth remembering.
lines: Given D.E is (1 + x²)dy/dx + y = e^(Tan⁻¹x)
This is in the form dy/dx + yP(x) = Q(x).
steps.why: Dividing every term by (1 + x²) makes the coefficient of dy/dx equal to 1, matching the standard linear form, and the resulting P is exactly the standard derivative-of-arctan integral.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to divide the right side e^(Tan⁻¹x) by (1 + x²) as well as the left side.
Confusing ∫1/(1+x²)dx with ∫1/√(1−x²)dx, which gives Sin⁻¹x instead.

steps.label: Find the integrating factor
steps.margin_note: One mark. I.F. = e^(∫P dx) always.
steps.memory_tip: Unlike the trig examples earlier in this chapter, this I.F. does not simplify further — e^(Tan⁻¹x) is already in its simplest form.
steps.why: Since ∫P dx = Tan⁻¹x here rather than a log expression, the integrating factor e^(Tan⁻¹x) does not simplify any further — it stays exactly as it is.
common_mistakes: Trying to simplify e^(Tan⁻¹x) further, as if it were e raised to a log.
Writing the I.F. as Tan⁻¹x, forgetting the e^(...) wrapper.

steps.label: Set up the integral and substitute
steps.margin_note: One mark. Multiplying two copies of e^(Tan⁻¹x) together gives e^(2Tan⁻¹x); the substitution t = Tan⁻¹x then removes the awkward exponent from the integral.
steps.memory_tip: e^A · e^A = e^(2A) — combine matching exponentials before attempting the integral.
lines: Hence the solution is y·(I.F.) = ∫(I.F.)Q dx
Put Tan⁻¹x = t ⇒ 1/(1 + x²) dx = dt,
steps.why: Multiplying the integrating factor by Q combines the two exponential terms into e^(2Tan⁻¹x), and substituting t = Tan⁻¹x removes the arctan from the exponent entirely, using the fact that dt is exactly the leftover 1/(1+x²)dx.
common_mistakes: Adding the exponents incorrectly, writing e^(Tan⁻¹x + Tan⁻¹x) as something other than e^(2Tan⁻¹x).
Forgetting that dt = 1/(1+x²) dx already matches the leftover factor exactly, and trying to substitute a different piece.

steps.label: Integrate and finish
steps.margin_note: The last mark. ∫e^(2t)dt = (1/2)e^(2t), then substitute t = Tan⁻¹x back in.
steps.memory_tip: ∫e^(kt)dt = e^(kt)/k for any constant k — here k = 2.
lines: and putting t = Tan⁻¹x back in:
steps.why: The standard rule for integrating an exponential of a constant multiple of t gives (1/2)e^(2t), and substituting t = Tan⁻¹x back in returns the final relation to the original variable x.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the 1/2 factor that comes from integrating e^(2t) rather than e^t.
Leaving the final answer in terms of t instead of substituting Tan⁻¹x back in.
